case_study_insert.main_stem: Thistledown Knitwear (TDK) is a private limited company in the fashion retail sector, selling knitwear online to UK customers and employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2016 by Priya Thistlewaite, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and ships its garments from a small Bristol warehouse. TDK plans to invest $420,000 in an automated knitting machine and a new e-commerce fulfilment warehouse, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and $170,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 15,000 units a year. TDK faces a rising defect rate of 4.2% on finished garments and growing customer complaints about late online deliveries.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce Operations Report — Q4 2025: TDK fulfilled 4,200 online orders last quarter, with a defect rate of 4.2% on finished garments, up from 2.6% a year ago. Customer complaints about late deliveries rose to 47 from 29 per month, and average dispatch time reached 3.4 days. A survey of 750 online shoppers found that 61% value free returns and 54% would pay more for locally made knitwear. A skills audit shows 9 of 32 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new knitting machines; off-the-job training at the local college costs $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thistledown Knitwear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of TDK's $250,000 variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.50 to $14.28 an hour from April 2026, raising payroll costs in the fulfilment warehouse. (3) Wool and synthetic fibre input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while online spending on fashion grew 4.3%.

questions.question_text: TDK is funding part of its $420,000 expansion with $170,000 retained profit rather than an additional bank loan. Explain two advantages for TDK of using retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so TDK keeps its cash flow intact while it installs the $420,000 automated knitting machine and fulfilment warehouse. With a $250,000 bank loan already committed and fixed costs of $180,000 a year, avoiding extra debt interest leaves more of the $38 selling price available to cover the $14 variable cost and absorb the 9.6% rise in fibre input costs.

Point 2: Using $170,000 of its own funds avoids the collateral and covenant conditions of a bank loan, so Priya Thistlewaite and the other shareholders keep full control of the e-commerce expansion and cannot face lender restrictions on how the warehouse is run. It is also quicker than arranging new borrowing, letting TDK respond to the 4.2% defect rate by fitting the new knitting machines immediately rather than waiting for lender approval. That speed helps protect the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who value free returns and keeps the growing base of online customers satisfied while the new fulfilment warehouse becomes operational.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TDK's expansion financing and cost position.

questions.question_text: TDK wants to grow online knitwear sales. Consider paid social media advertising, fashion influencer marketing, or a search-engine advertising campaign. Which should TDK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Paid social media advertising: Platforms such as Instagram and TikTok let TDK target UK knitwear shoppers by interest and age, and short videos can show garment quality to the 54% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay more for locally made knitwear. Costs are controllable and results are measurable against the 4,200-order baseline. However, competition for attention is intense, and with $420,000 already committed to the expansion and a $250,000 bank loan, a poorly targeted campaign can waste spend quickly.

Fashion influencer marketing: Reviews by knitwear and sustainable-fashion influencers would give credible endorsement to TDK's locally made positioning, reaching the 61% of shoppers who value free returns and building trust faster than brand-owned adverts. Engagement can be tracked, but good influencers charge high fees, outcomes depend on their reputation, and one negative review about the current 4.2% defect rate could damage the brand just as the new machine is installed.

Search-engine advertising: Shopping adverts appear exactly when a customer searches for a wool cardigan, capturing high-intent buyers and driving immediate traffic to the e-commerce warehouse. They are measurable and scale with budget, but cost-per-click in fashion is high, they do little to build long-term brand loyalty, and they cannot show texture or quality as well as video; the 4.2% defect problem would also show up as returns.

Recommendation: TDK should choose paid social media advertising, reinforced later by a small influencer pilot. Social adverts reach the precise online audience at controllable cost, demonstrate the garments visually, and can be evaluated against the 4.2% defect rate and the 47 late-delivery complaints as the new fulfilment warehouse beds in. Influencer marketing is rejected as the main channel because fees and reputation risk are high for a firm with $180,000 fixed costs; search-engine advertising is rejected as a primary approach because it wins clicks but not the loyalty or brand story the 54% premium segment wants. A phased social campaign protects cash while the $420,000 investment starts delivering.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TDK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TDK with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why influencer marketing and search advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: TDK's defect rate has reached 4.2% and complaints about late deliveries are rising. Explain two benefits for TDK of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 32.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the workforce of 32, especially those packing and dispatching online orders, to suggest fixes for the 4.2% defect rate and the late-delivery complaints. Because these staff handle the garments every day, their ideas on machine settings and packing routines are practical, and being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which reduces errors and rework on the new automated knitting machine.

Point 2: Involvement strengthens TDK's flat organisational structure by giving workers ownership of quality, so the 47 monthly complaints about late deliveries can be tackled through team suggestions on dispatch scheduling rather than top-down instructions alone. Higher morale also supports the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who value free returns: engaged staff check garments more carefully, cutting the 4.2% defect rate and the $700-per-employee retraining cost linked to replacing dissatisfied workers, while output of 15,000 units a year is maintained.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TDK's defect rate, complaints, structure and output.

questions.question_text: TDK must train 9 of 32 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new knitting machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TDK choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the knitting machines is directly relevant to TDK's own equipment and quality checks, costs no course fees, and keeps the 9 trainees productive while the 4,200-order quarter is fulfilled. Supervisors can correct the errors behind the 4.2% defect rate immediately and link training to the 47 late-delivery complaints. The drawbacks are that experienced operators lose time teaching, bad habits may be copied, and there is no external certificate to evidence competence.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $700 per employee costs 9 × $700 = $6,300, a modest sum against the $420,000 investment. It provides structured, certified machine skills and removes trainees from distractions, which matters when defects are rising. However, it takes 9 of a workforce of 32 away from the warehouse during a busy quarter, risking slower dispatch and more late-delivery complaints, and the generic syllabus may not match TDK's exact machines without follow-up coaching.

Decision: TDK should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short certified college modules later for senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids worsening the 47 complaints while the flat structure and democratic leadership already support peer coaching. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because $6,300 and nine lost shifts would disrupt the 15,000-unit output at a sensitive launch. A pilot on one machine group should compare the 4.2% defect rate before extending training, with Priya Thistlewaite reviewing whether the $700 fee is later justified.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TDK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of TDK.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TDK's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($38 − $14) = $180,000 ÷ $24 = 7,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 7,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38 − $14 = $24. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TDK's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 7,500-unit break-even point with actual output of 15,000 units gives a margin of safety of 7,500 units, showing how far online demand can fall before TDK stops covering its $180,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets managers model a discount: cutting the $38 price by $2 to $36 leaves $22 contribution, so they can judge whether extra orders from the 61% who value free returns would still be profitable.
3. With a $250,000 bank loan to service, the $24 contribution and 15,000-unit output show the annual surplus available for repayments, guiding how quickly the $420,000 expansion can be funded from cash flow.
4. Unit cost can be benchmarked as $180,000 ÷ 15,000 = $12 plus $14 variable cost = $26 a garment, letting TDK track whether the 4.2% defect rate and the $700 training spend are pushing costs above target each quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 7,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 7,500-unit margin of safety against 15,000 output; discount pricing from $38 using $24 contribution; servicing the $250,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $26 against the 4.2% defect rate and $700 training cost.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TDK's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TDK's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.30 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $80,000 + $50,000 = $200,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50 and ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75. For 2025, $200,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.00 and ($200,000 − $70,000) ÷ $100,000 = $130,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.30.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has strengthened on both measures. The first measure rose from 1.50 to 2.00 even though trade receivables increased from $60,000 to $80,000, because cash doubled from $30,000 to $50,000 and current liabilities fell from $120,000 to $100,000. The second measure, which strips out stock, climbed from 0.75 to 1.30 and is the more important signal here: TDK can now meet its short-term bills without relying on selling the $70,000 of knitwear inventory, which is valuable while it services a $250,000 loan and spends $420,000 on the new fulfilment warehouse. The reservation is that trade receivables have risen by $20,000, tying up cash that could otherwise fund the 9.6% fibre-input increase; if online customers or wholesale accounts pay late, the stronger position could weaken quickly.

Conclusion: TDK's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the improvement does not depend on inventory, so the business is better placed to meet its obligations. Rising receivables are the main residual risk, so tighter credit control should accompany the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the financial position.

questions.question_text: TDK is considering a free-returns policy for its online knitwear. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TDK of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A free-returns policy directly answers the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who value free returns, reducing a barrier to buying knitwear online and supporting the $38 selling price and $24 contribution on each garment. Higher conversion on the 4,200-order baseline would spread the $180,000 fixed costs over more units and help justify the $420,000 fulfilment investment.

Disadvantage: Free returns create reverse-logistics costs and can be abused, which would raise the $14 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins, especially as the defect rate is already 4.2% and may generate avoidable returns. The insert gives no figure for the cost of handling a return or for how much sales would rise, so the net effect cannot be quantified; the decision must be judged qualitatively. TDK should trial the policy on a single product line and compare return rates and the 47 monthly complaints before extending it nationally, keeping the $250,000 loan commitment in mind.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TDK's survey, costs, defect rate and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in fibre input costs will affect TDK. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If TDK's $250,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $250,000 = $1,875 a year (0.0075 × $250,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $180,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it altogether. The higher rate could still make future borrowing for the $420,000 expansion dearer and slightly dampen the 4.3% growth in online fashion spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.28 an hour): The workforce of 32 includes hourly-paid packing and warehouse staff, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 15,000 units ÷ 32 staff = 468.75 garments per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; reducing the 4.2% defect rate and training the 9 untrained staff would help sustain it.

Fibre input costs (9.6%): These feed the $14 variable cost on every garment. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $14 were exposed, 9.6% × $14 = $1.344, about $1.34 a unit, and at 15,000 units that is roughly $20,160 a year (15,000 × $1.344). Even a smaller exposed share erodes the $24 contribution, and it recurs on every unit.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in fibre input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 15,000 garments and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $250,000 loan and funds the $420,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,875 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 468.75 garments per worker. TDK should cut the 4.2% defect rate and review the $38 price rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TDK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TDK's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that fibre input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
